interpretation: A cold acquisition email for independent repair shop owners who are considering ways for customers to inspect repair stages. It should introduce Repairboard and invite a low-commitment inspection of the sample board, without implying the reader has begun a software project or already uses another system.
reader:
Selected audience (user-stated constraints): Independent repair shop owners considering how customers can inspect repair stages..
No further recipient situation is established. Compiled market context is research to check for applicability, not a replacement biography.
reader_segment: Independent repair shop owners considering how customers can inspect repair stages.
reader_profile_override: Independent repair shop owners considering how customers can inspect repair stages.
promise: The reader can inspect Repairboard's shared-stage and read-only customer-view mechanism before deciding whether it fits how their shop wants to present repair status.
orientation: Repairboard is a shared board that displays each repair's current stage and lets a shop share a read-only status link with its customer.
arc: In one email, move from a plain introduction of the product to its customer-facing mechanism, then invite the reader to inspect a sample and judge its relevance.
sequence_rationale: One self-contained email matches the explicit request. Because no customer results, pains, current workflow, pricing, setup details, or integrations are established, the argument rests on the documented mechanism and an inspectable first step rather than urgency, replacement claims, or social proof.

emails.job: Get a cold repair shop owner to view the sample board and decide whether this way of presenting repair stages is relevant to their shop.
emails.single_idea: Repairboard provides a shared view of each repair's current stage while giving customers a read-only way to inspect status.
emails.felt_need: I want customers to be able to inspect where a repair stands.
emails.mechanism: Repairboard displays each repair's current stage on a shared board, and the shop can share a read-only status link with its customer.
emails.belief_shift: Before: the reader does not know what Repairboard is or how it presents repair status. After: the reader understands the shared-board and read-only-link mechanism and can inspect a sample to judge whether it suits their shop.
must_not_say: Do not claim reduced calls, saved time, increased trust, higher satisfaction, faster repairs, or any other customer result.
Do not imply the reader currently uses spreadsheets, phone updates, another product, or any particular status workflow.
Do not imply the reader has scoped, started, delayed, or abandoned a software project.
Do not claim easy setup, migration, integrations, automation, notifications, security, pricing, a free plan, or a trial.
Do not claim customer adoption, testimonials, market leadership, uniqueness, or superiority to alternatives.
Do not describe the link as customer-specific, real-time, branded, secure, or tied to notifications; only say it is read-only and can be shared with a customer.
emails.objection: A customer-facing status view should not give the customer editing access; the documented link is read-only.
emails.tone: Matter-of-fact, concise, and invitational rather than sales-heavy.
emails.next_step_decision: Decide whether Repairboard's way of presenting repair stages is relevant enough to investigate further for the shop.
emails.next_step_value: The sample lets the reader inspect the repair-board presentation described in the email instead of relying only on the claim.
emails.next_step_limit: Viewing the sample does not establish setup effort, integrations, pricing, production fit, or how the board would work with the shop's existing processes.
emails.subject_strategy: Earn the open by plainly signaling a customer-visible repair-status view or sample, without promising an outcome or implying an existing software initiative.
